blocks.content: This topic gives the honest, real guidance on provisioners, a genuine last resort, reached for only when no native Terraform or provider mechanism already exists for the same goal.
1. A Genuine Last Resort
The honest, real framing worth internalizing, provisioners are genuinely a last resort, not a default, everyday tool reached for casually whenever a resource needs some setup.
Every topic so far in this module has been building toward this one, honest conclusion, understanding provisioners well is precisely what makes it possible to use them sparingly and deliberately.
This framing is not about avoiding a genuinely useful tool out of excessive caution, it is about matching the tool to situations that actually, genuinely need it.
Keep this framing in mind through the rest of this topic, it is the lens every piece of guidance that follows is filtered through.

blocks.content: 2. Check for a Native Mechanism First
blocks.text: 2. Check for a Native Mechanism First

blocks.content: Before reaching for remote-exec to configure a fresh VM, check whether a native, provider-level mechanism already exists, AWS's user_data, for instance, is often a genuinely better fit for exactly this same goal.
Native mechanisms are generally tracked more cleanly by the provider itself, avoiding the real connection fragility and lack of drift detection covered throughout this module.
This check genuinely takes only a few minutes, searching the relevant provider's documentation for the specific goal at hand, before writing a single line of provisioner configuration.
Making this check a real, habitual first step is one of the single most effective ways to keep provisioner usage genuinely rare and deliberate.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784539147992-186528956.png
blocks.alt: A real, native alternative, genuinely worth checking for before reaching for a provisioner

blocks.content: 3. When They Genuinely Make Sense
Provisioners genuinely make sense when no native alternative exists at all for a specific, real need, not simply when they happen to be a convenient, familiar option.
This threshold is deliberately strict, familiarity or convenience alone are genuinely not enough justification, the real, honest bar is the absence of any native alternative.
Applying this threshold consistently across a real team keeps provisioner usage rare enough that each individual instance remains genuinely well understood and reviewed.
When the threshold is met honestly, the topics covered earlier in this module become the real, practical reference for using the right provisioner correctly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784539149564-743141655.png

4. A Reasonable Real Case
A genuinely one-off bootstrapping step, with no equivalent native mechanism available, is a reasonable, real case where a provisioner is a defensible, deliberate choice.

The key word here is genuinely one-off, a repeated, ongoing configuration need is a much stronger signal that a dedicated configuration-management tool, not a provisioner, is the right, honest answer.
A real example might be triggering a genuinely external, one-time registration call that has no Terraform-native equivalent at all, anywhere in the relevant provider.
Even in a reasonable case like this, documenting directly in the code why a provisioner was chosen is worth the small, real effort for whoever reads it next.

blocks.content: 5. Creation-Time vs Destroy-Time
Provisioners can also run specifically when a resource is destroyed, using when = destroy, a rarer, real distinction from the default creation-time behavior already covered.
A destroy-time provisioner genuinely runs before the resource is actually removed, useful for a real, final cleanup step that has no native equivalent.
This is genuinely rarer in practice than creation-time provisioners, and worth exactly the same honest scrutiny, is there truly no native way to achieve this same cleanup.
A destroy-time provisioner that itself fails can genuinely complicate a real destroy operation, worth testing carefully before relying on it in production.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784539152873-785025301.png
blocks.alt: A rarer, real timing option, running specifically as a resource is being destroyed

blocks.content: 6. A Real Team Practice
Any real, genuine use of a provisioner in a team's codebase is worth a deliberate review, why a native mechanism did not fit, and what the honest fallback plan is if it fails.
Treating a provisioner's addition with the same real scrutiny as any other meaningful architectural decision keeps its use genuinely rare and well justified over time.
A short comment directly in the code, explaining why no native alternative existed, is a genuinely small but valuable habit worth adopting as a team.
This real practice also makes it easier to revisit and remove a provisioner later, if a native alternative eventually does become available.

7. A Practical Checklist
Before adding any provisioner, working through a short, honest checklist genuinely helps avoid reaching for one out of habit rather than real necessity.
This checklist deliberately echoes the individual checklists already given for each provisioner earlier in this module, now brought together at the level of the decision itself.
Running through it consistently, every single time, is what keeps provisioner usage genuinely rare rather than gradually creeping back into habit.
A team that applies this checklist honestly will naturally end up with very few provisioners in its real, production codebase.

blocks.content: 9. A Real Alternative: Configuration Management
For genuinely ongoing configuration needs, beyond a true one-off bootstrapping step, a dedicated configuration-management tool is generally the more honest, appropriate real answer.
These tools are built specifically for exactly this job, tracking real, ongoing configuration state in a way provisioners genuinely are not designed to do.
Recognizing this distinction, one-off bootstrapping versus ongoing configuration, is genuinely one of the clearest signals for whether a provisioner is truly appropriate at all.
This distinction resurfaces directly in the next, final topic of this module, alongside the deeper, real reasons behind it.

blocks.content: 11. A Real, Worked Example
Walking through one real, concrete scenario end to end makes this threshold easier to apply consistently than reading the guidance alone.
Imagine a team needing a freshly created database instance registered with an internal, legacy inventory system that has no Terraform provider at all.
Checking first, genuinely, confirms no native resource or data source covers this internal system, satisfying the real threshold from earlier in this topic.
A local-exec provisioner, calling that internal system's own API directly, becomes a reasonable, deliberate, and honestly documented choice in this specific, real case.

blocks.content: 12. When the Native Alternative Appears Later
blocks.text: 12. When the Native Alternative Appears Later

blocks.content: Provider ecosystems genuinely evolve, a native mechanism that did not exist when a provisioner was first added may genuinely exist later.
This is precisely why the team-review practice covered earlier in this topic recommends documenting the original reasoning directly in the code.
Revisiting existing provisioners periodically, checking whether a native alternative has genuinely since appeared, is a small, worthwhile habit.
Replacing a provisioner with a newly available native mechanism is a genuinely worthwhile improvement, not a purely cosmetic change.

The honest threshold covered throughout this topic, genuinely no native alternative, and genuinely one-off, is deliberately strict for good, real reasons.
Applying it consistently is what keeps a real, production Terraform codebase close to the reliable, declarative model the next topic explains in full.
This topic's guidance is the practical half of this module's conclusion, the final topic supplies the deeper, concrete reasoning behind it.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Provisioners are a genuine last resort, check for a native mechanism, like AWS user_data, before reaching for remote-exec.
They genuinely make sense only when no native alternative exists at all for a specific, often one-off need, worth a deliberate team review.
when = destroy runs a provisioner specifically at destroy time, and ongoing configuration needs are better served by dedicated configuration-management tools.
